newsitem.title: USA: Dad of Megan's killer says he should die - NY Times.
newsitem.headline: Dad of Megan's killer says he should die - NY Times.

text.p: The father of Jesse Timmendequas said his son should die for killing 7-year-old Megan Kanka and denied allegations he sexually abused him, The New York Times reported Thursday.

Jesse Timmendequas was convicted last month of the 1994 attack on Megan, which inspired "Megan's Law." It required child molesters to register with police when they moved into a town and was much copied around the United States.

Timmendequas' father, Edward James Howard, said testimony by Jesse's brother Paul that he physically and sexually abused his son were being used to excuse Jesse for a crime that deserved the death penalty.
"He definitely should be killed," Howard, 70, said in an interview at his home in Smoketree Valley, a collection of trailers in the Southern California desert.
"... My dad kicked the hell out of me from the time I was able to walk. I didn't kill a baby. So when they say it's mommy's fault or daddy's fault, it's just an excuse," he told the Times.

Timmendequas' trial in Trenton, N.J., was in the fourth day of its penalty phase Thursday. Defence attorneys hope to keep Jesse Timmendequas from being executed by portraying a hellish childhood of abuse and neglect they contend made him mentally ill.

Prosecutors in Mercer County Superior Court hammered at testimony by Carol Krych, a forensic social worker hired by the defence to explore Timmendequas' family background. Krych arranged for Paul Timmendequas' testiony and acknowledged there was no documentation for his allegations of abuse.
Paul Timmendequas, 33, said in videotaped testimony this week that his father sexually and physically abused him and his brother. Howard denied the allegations, the Times said.
"It's all lies. All of it," said Howard, who said he was in prison for burglary while Jesse was a little boy and then left the family a year afterward.
"Lawyers are saying all kinds of things about me. Well, if all that happened, why didn't they call any witnesses during the trial?"

Despite his testimony, Paul Timmendequas has told The Newark Star-Ledger he would like to help execute his brother. No member of the Timmendequas family has appeared at his trial in Mercer County Superior Court.
Prosecutors are seeking the death penalty. Under a new state law, Timmendequas could be sentenced to life in prison without parole.
